items.context:
Your pipeline is one long function. The table it returns has one column
of obviously wrong numbers.

Why is that hard to track down?
items.why:
Stages give you a seam at every boundary. You open the output of load,
then of clean, then of aggregate, and the first one that looks wrong
tells you which step to fix. One long function has no such seam, so
every question about the middle costs you a full re-run with prints
added.
items.true: No step saved its output, so there is nothing to inspect
false: The bug has to be in the last step that ran
You cannot put print statements inside a function
Pandas hides intermediate results on purpose

items.context:
You `scan_parquet` a table of 55 columns, select 6 of them, then
`.collect()`.

How many columns come off the disk?
items.why:
This is projection pushdown. Because `scan_parquet` builds a plan
instead of reading immediately, your later `.select()` folds back into
the read itself, so the 49 columns you never asked for are never pulled
off the disk. DuckDB did the same thing to Parquet in Lecture 4, from
inside a database. Polars does it with no server involved.
items.true: 6: the selection folds into the read
false: 55, and then 49 are dropped
55, because a scan always reads everything
6, but only if you select by position

items.context: What do you give up by running Polars in lazy mode?
items.why:
A bad expression may not raise until `.collect()`, several lines and
sometimes several stages away from the line that caused it. Eager pandas
would have failed on the offending line instead. That is a real
debugging cost, and it is why exploratory work often stays eager and
the lazy version comes later, once the pipeline has settled.
items.true: Errors surface at `.collect()`, far from their cause
false: Memory, because the plan is held in full
Repeatability, because the optimizer reorders steps
Column types, until the data is loaded

items.context: When should you stay with pandas instead of switching to Polars?
items.why:
Polars is stricter, and that costs you while you are still learning it:
more of your mistakes turn into real errors instead of quiet
workarounds. The deciding factor is usually who else has to read your
code. Plotting is not a reason to avoid Polars, because converting
between the two is cheap.
items.true: When your codebase or coworkers only use pandas
false: When the whole table already fits in memory
When the transformations are fairly simple
When you need to plot the result afterwards

items.context:
A stage saves its result as `clean.parquet`. You change a setting that
stage depends on and run the pipeline again.

What do you get?
items.why:
Nothing links `clean.parquet` to the setting that produced it, so
nothing marks it stale and the next run quietly reads it back. Name the
cache after the inputs and settings that determine its contents, so a
changed setting produces a different filename and the old one can never
be mistaken for current.
items.true: The old file, because its name ignores the setting
false: A fresh result, because the setting is an input
An error, because the schema no longer matches
Two files, and the newer one is used

items.context:
One `for` loop over a column of 480,000 readings, against the same test
done on the whole column at once.

Before you look: how much slower is the loop?
items.why:
Measured on the reactor-pressure column, 480,000 readings: the
whole-column comparison takes 0.2 ms, a plain `for` loop about 20 ms,
and the same thing written with `iterrows()` about 3,900 ms. The
whole-column version hands the work to compiled code once; the loop
pays Python's per-row cost 480,000 times. Which loop you write matters
as much as whether you write one at all.
false: About five times slower
About the same speed
Only slower on bigger data

items.context:
You have one row per reading. You want one row per fault, with each
sensor averaged over that fault.

Which operation gets you there?
items.why:
This is `GROUP BY faultNumber` from Lecture 3, written as a method call
instead of a clause: `readings.group_by("faultNumber").agg(...)`. A join
matches rows across two tables, a filter throws rows away, and a sort
reorders them. None of the three collapses many rows into one summary
per group, which is the job here.
items.true: group_by on faultNumber, then agg with mean
false: join on faultNumber, then agg with mean
filter on faultNumber, then agg with mean
sort by faultNumber, then agg with mean

items.context: What does it mean to say a stage is idempotent?
items.why:
The payoff is that you can retry. You do not have to work out whether
the last attempt finished, or what it left behind: you just run the
stage again. A database's transactions gave you this for free, and a
plain Python pipeline has to rebuild it by hand.
items.true: Running it twice does what running it once does
false: It takes the same time on any input size
It keeps no state between two runs
It never leaves a half-written file

items.context:
Run the pandas-against-Polars benchmark in
[`l05-pipelines.ipynb`](../lectures/l05/l05-pipelines.ipynb).

What does the number you get tell you?
items.why:
One laptop, one dataset, one set of operations. Run the same comparison
on a different pipeline and the ratio moves. What does carry over is
the gap between a loop and a whole-column operation, because that comes
from the shape of the computation rather than from which library you
picked. So measure your own pipeline before you rewrite it.
items.true: How these operations run on this machine, and little else
false: That Polars should replace pandas in your work
That the two are the same once you allow for noise
That timing a pipeline is not worth doing
